title: Panja Sahib
hookLine: the gurdwara of the handprint at Hasan Abdal

cards: Clear water slides out from under a rock, into a stone channel, and on into a wide tank where fish turn lazily in the light.
One by one, pilgrims kneel, reach out, and fit a hand into a shape pressed into the rock above the water. Some hold it there a long moment. Some laugh because their hand is smaller.
Some close their eyes. This is Hasan Abdal, in the hills of northern Pakistan, and the gurdwara is Panja Sahib. Year one told the story of the rock.

teach.b: First, the story in one breath. Tradition says Guru Nanak and Mardana came to the hill thirsty.

Mardana climbed three times to ask for water from the spring of a holy man at the top, Wali Qandhari, and three times came down with nothing. Nanak had him lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and water came up.
A boulder came rolling down. Nanak stopped it with his open palm, and his hand, the story says, stayed in the stone. Panja means the palm of the hand.
Refused at the top, it came up at the bottom, where the thirsty men sat, and it still flows there today, under the handprint and past the pilgrims. Third, why water matters so much here.

teach.h: ONE GIVER FOR EVERY LIVING BEING.
teach.b: In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that the Guru has given him one understanding: there is one giver for every living being, and may he never forget that one.
Water is about as plain a gift as there is, and in the story nobody owns the giver. Fourth, how to hold the hilltop. Sikhs read this story in more than one way, some as a miracle, some as a picture.

teach.h: A SHRINE ABOVE, A GURDWARA BELOW.
teach.b: People remember Wali Qandhari differently from the story, and a shrine to him still stands on the hill above, where visitors climb too.

So the place keeps both: a shrine on the hill, a gurdwara at its foot, and water running between. What a pilgrim takes away is the shape of the hand: open, steady, where the thirsty were given a drink.

how: Pilgrims who visit Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal place their hands in the handprint on the rock and take water from the spring that flows beneath it.

o: the gurdwara honoring the five beloved ones of the Khalsa
a shrine to the holy man on the hilltop above
the gurdwara of Guru Nanak's handprint in the rock

s: at Panja Sahib the water flows from the top of the hill
in the story it was refused above and came up below, and it still flows under the handprint.
pilgrims fit their hands into the print on the rock
they kneel at the water's edge and place a hand in the shape.
the hilltop shrine to Wali Qandhari is gone
it still stands on the hill above the gurdwara, and visitors climb to it too.

games.q: you're Mardana. three times you've climbed for water and come down with nothing. Nanak tells you to lift a stone at the foot of the hill. what comes up?
o: a coin to buy a drink.
games.why: tradition says water came up from under the stone, at the bottom of the hill where the thirsty men were. it still flows there today.

practice: Lay one hand flat on a table, your knee, or the floor, fingers spread, nothing gripped. Breathe in and notice it's steady; breathe out and notice it's open.
Keep the palm open while you think of someone thirsty for something you could give: time, a call, a glass of water, a kind word.

wordCard.voice: Panja Sahib. The gurdwara at Hasan Abdal where pilgrims fit their hands into the print of Guru Nanak's palm, with water flowing beneath it. Today's word.

orig.note: panja, the palm of the hand: the gurdwara named for the handprint in the rock.

carryVoice: Your line: the handprint. An open hand, low enough to reach the thirsty. One more day on the hill.
